::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Graph of $f(x,y)=i$](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4739533/graph-of-fx-y-i), asked by user1179665 on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-07-20; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Let $f:\Bbb{R}^2\longrightarrow \Bbb{R}$ and $f(x,y)=i.$
>
> So will the graph of this function be x-y plane? 
> Where it has 3 axis: x and y are real axis and z is the imaginary axis?
> Basically somewhat like [Is this the Graph][q-1]
>
>
>   [q-1]: cDyxc.png
>
>
> I am in highschool and I was just curious because my teachers'answer wasn't satisfactory enough.
:::

The best way I can understand your function is from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{C}$. Both are two-dimensional vector spaces over $\mathbb{R}$, so the graph lies in the four-dimensional space $\mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{C}$. It is
$$A = \left\{(x,y,i) \mid x,y \in \mathbb{R} \right\}$$
It is a two-dimensional affine plane lying in four-dimensional space.

If you ignore one of those dimensions, you might be able to “see” the graph better. Replace $\mathbb{C}$ with $\mathbb{R}$ and $i$ with $1$. The graph of $f(x,y) = 1$ lies in three-dimensional space, and it's just the $xy$-plane shifted “up” by one unit. The graph of your complex $f$ is the same $xy$-plane shifted one in the $i$ direction.
